statement: Fully fissioning one kilogram of U-235 releases about 82 terajoules of heat.
detail: At about 200 MeV per fission: 22.8 GWh of heat, or roughly 2,800 tonnes of coal equivalent at 29.3 GJ each.

unit: GJ heat per kg natural U
statement: A kilogram of mined uranium yields about 450 GJ of heat in today's reactors.
detail: WNA reference cycle (4.5% fuel, 0.22% tails, 45 GWd/t): about 41,500 kWh of electricity, some 19,000 times coal at 24 MJ/kg.
calc: 24.3 tU fuel x 45 GWd/t x 86,400 GJ/GWd / 211,000 kg natural U = 448 GJ/kg; 8.76 TWh / 211 tU = 41,517 kWh(e)/kg; 447,765 MJ / 24 MJ = 18,657x coal. WNA rounds to 44 million kWh per tonne.

statement: One kilogram of enriched reactor fuel generates about 360,000 kWh of electricity.
detail: At 45 GWd/t burn-up and one-third efficiency. A lithium-ion battery stores roughly 0.1 to 0.24 kWh per kilogram per charge.
calc: 45,000 MWd/t = 45 MWd/kg; x 24 h x 1,000 kWh/MWh / 3 = 360,000 kWh(e) per kg U. Li-ion 0.36-0.875 MJ/kg / 3.6 = 0.10-0.24 kWh/kg.

statement: Reactor fuel holds roughly 100,000 times more energy per kilogram than coal or oil.
detail: Megajoules per kg: Li-ion battery 0.4-0.9, coal 24-35, oil 41.9, natural gas 53.6, reactor fuel 3.9 million, fully fissioned U-235 82 million.

statement: One fingertip-sized uranium fuel pellet holds the heat of roughly a tonne of coal.
detail: A 7 g pellet at 45 GWd/t releases 24 GJ, matching 1 t of 24 MJ/kg coal; a 5 g pellet, about 0.7 t.
calc: 7 g UO2 x 0.8815 = 6.17 g U; x 45 GWd/t = 24.0 GJ = 1.00 t coal at 24 MJ/kg (0.82 tce). 5 g pellet: 17.1 GJ = 0.71 t.

statement: About five to seven fuel pellets cover an average US home's electricity for a year.
detail: A 7 g pellet yields about 2,200 kWh at 45 GWd/t and one-third efficiency; EIA's average home bought 10,791 kWh in 2022.
calc: 6.17 g U x 360 kWh/g = 2,221 kWh; 10,791 / 2,221 = 4.9 pellets (7 g) or 6.8 pellets (5 g)

statement: One uranium fission releases about 50 million times the energy of burning one carbon atom.
detail: Roughly 200 million electron-volts per U-235 fission against about 4 electron-volts per carbon atom oxidised in coal, oil or gas.

statement: A 1 GWe reactor converts about one kilogram of mass into energy each year.
detail: 26.2 TWh of heat divided by c squared. Roughly 1.15 tonnes of heavy atoms fission to release it, about 3 kg a day.
calc: 24.3 tU x 45 GWd/t = 26.24 TWh heat = 9.448e+16 J; / c^2 = 1.05 kg; / 8.210e+13 J/kg = 1,151 kg fissioned = 3.15 kg/day

statement: One reactor-year: 249 t of yellowcake becomes 27.6 t of fuel and 8.76 TWh.
detail: 1 GWe light-water reactor at full output: 4.5% enrichment, 0.22% tails, 45 GWd/t. At a 90% load factor, about 190 tU.

flow.note: WNA figure; the ideal-cascade formula with 0.711% feed gives about 178,000
100% output; about 7.9 TWh at 90% load factor
about 26 t uranium, 1 t fission products, 0.28 t transuranics

statement: Enriching one reactor-year of fuel takes about 180,000 separative work units.
detail: 24.3 tU to 4.5% at 0.22% tails is 7.3 SWU per kg by the standard formula; WNA quotes 182,000. A 5%, 65 GWd/t cycle: about 140,000.

statement: Nearly 90% of mined uranium ends up as depleted tails, never entering a reactor.
detail: Of 211 tU fed to enrichment for one reactor-year, 24.3 tU becomes 4.5% fuel; 187 tU remains at 0.22% U-235.

unit: kg natural U per kg fuel
statement: Each kilogram of 4.5% fuel needs 8.7 kg of natural uranium and 7.3 SWU.
detail: At 0.22% tails. For 5% fuel: 9.4 kg and 8.9 SWU at 0.20% tails, or 10.3 kg and 7.9 SWU at 0.25%.

statement: A new reactor's first core needs about three years' worth of fuel at once.
detail: The reference 1 GWe core holds 73 tU against 24.3 tU reloaded yearly; WNA puts first loads at 300-450 t natural uranium.
calc: 73 / 24.3 = 3.00; in natural-uranium terms 300-450 tU vs ~150 tU/yr = 2-3x

statement: 1 kg of uranium equals 2.6 lb of U3O8; 1 lb U3O8 holds 0.385 kg U.
detail: U3O8 is 84.8% uranium by mass. One tonne of uranium is 2,599.8 lb U3O8; a million pounds U3O8 is 384.6 tU.

statement: Only about half a percent of mined uranium is actually fissioned in today's reactors.
detail: About 1.15 t fissions per reactor-year out of 211 tU mined. Within the fuel, 45 GWd/t burns under 5% of heavy atoms.
calc: 1,151 kg / 211,000 kg = 0.55%; fuel burn-up 45 / 950 GWd/t = 4.7% of heavy atoms

statement: Enriching a reactor's fuel uses about 0.1% of the electricity that fuel will generate.
detail: About 182,000 SWU at roughly 50 kWh each in centrifuges is 9 GWh against 8.76 TWh. Old diffusion plants needed 2,500 kWh per SWU.

statement: A 1 GWe reactor uses about 11,400 tonnes of natural uranium over 60 years.
detail: 190 tU a year at a 90% load factor: about 30 million lb U3O8 over 60 years, nearly 40 million over 80.

statement: Natural uranium is 99.27% U-238, 0.72% U-235 and 0.005% U-234.
detail: Atom fractions. Half-lives: U-238 about 4.47 billion years, U-235 704 million, U-234 245,500. By weight, U-235 is 0.711%.

statement: From 0.7% U-235 in the ground to 5% in reactors and over 90% in weapons.
detail: LEU is under 20% (power reactors 3-5%); LEU+ 5-10%; HALEU 5-20%; HEU 20% and up; weapons-grade over 90%.

statement: A one-litre carton of uranium metal would weigh 19 kilograms.
detail: Density 19.05 g/cm3 at 20 C, about 19 times water. Sources quote anything from 18.7 to 19.1.

statement: A year's uranium for a 1 GWe reactor would form a 1.1-metre metal cube.
detail: 24.3 tonnes of enriched uranium at 19.05 t per cubic metre is 1.28 cubic metres. The 211 tU mined for it: a 2.2-metre cube.

statement: All the uranium the world's reactors need in a year fits a 15-metre cube.
detail: 68,920 tU required in 2025 (WNA); as solid metal at 19.05 t per cubic metre, about 3,600 cubic metres.

statement: Two billion years ago natural uranium was about 3.7% U-235, like today's reactor fuel.
detail: U-235 decays over six times faster than U-238, so ore was once rich enough for the Oklo natural reactors.

statement: Uranium is about as common as tin: 2.7 parts per million of Earth's crust.
detail: Handbook values: tin 2.3 ppm, silver 0.075, gold 0.004. That makes uranium roughly 36 times silver and 700 times gold.

statement: The oceans hold more than four billion tonnes of dissolved uranium.
detail: At about 3.3 parts per billion: roughly 700 times identified land resources, but far costlier to extract.
calc: 1.335e9 km3 of seawater x 1.025 t/m3 x 3.3e-9 = 4.5 billion t; / 5.86 million tU = 770x. PNNL: 'more than four billion tons'.

statement: Canada's Cigar Lake ore averages 16% uranium oxide; Namibia's Rössing ore, 0.03% uranium.
detail: About 420 times richer. One reactor-year's 211 tU means 1,500 t of Cigar Lake ore or 640,000 t at Rössing.

statement: Identified uranium resources would cover about 85 years of today's reactor demand.
detail: 5.86 million tU recoverable below $130 per kg (January 2025) against 68,920 tU a year. Australia holds 29% of it.

statement: 444 operable power reactors worldwide total 407 GWe; 81 more are under construction.
detail: WNA count on 17 November 2026, across 31 countries. The US has the most (94), then China (65) and France (57).

statement: Nuclear generated a record 2,702 TWh in 2025: about 9% of the world's electricity.
detail: Ember puts it at 8.9%, down from 16.6% in 2000. That is about a fifth of all low-carbon electricity.

statement: Reactors need about 179 million pounds of U3O8 a year; mines produced 157 million.
detail: 68,920 tU required in 2025; 60,213 tU mined in 2024, about 90% of that year's needs. Stockpiles and recycling fill the gap.

statement: Three countries mine 75% of the world's uranium; Kazakhstan alone accounts for 39%.
detail: 2024: Kazakhstan 23,270 tU, Canada 14,309, Namibia 7,333, of 60,213 tU. In-situ leaching delivered 55% of world output.

statement: Just five mines produce 42% of the world's uranium; the top ten produce 62%.
detail: 2024: McArthur River/Key Lake 13%, Cigar Lake 11%, Husab 7%, Karatau 6%, Inkai 5%. Kazatomprom, Cameco and Orano mined 49%.

statement: Rosatom holds 43% of world enrichment capacity; four suppliers hold over 99%.
detail: 2025, million SWU: Rosatom 29.1, Urenco 17.3, CNNC 13.8, Orano 7.5 of 68.1. Conversion comes from just five companies.

statement: Uranium is 45% of nuclear fuel cost, and under 10% of a new plant's total cost.
detail: WNA, November 2026 prices: fuel costs $3,950 per kg, or 1.1 cents per kWh. Fuel is 15-20% of new-plant costs.

statement: Doubling the uranium price adds only about $5 to a nuclear megawatt-hour.
detail: $1,780 of uranium per kg of fuel, spread over 360,000 kWh. A gas plant's cost moves about $6/MWh per 10% fuel-price change.
calc: $1,780 / 360,000 kWh = $4.94/MWh extra if uranium doubles (from ~$91/lb U3O8). WNA's older example: $25 -> $50/lb lifts fuel cost 0.50 -> 0.62 c/kWh.

statement: US reactors ran at a 91% capacity factor in 2025; the world fleet averaged 84%.
detail: EIA: between 90.8% and 93.4% every year since 2019, against wind 33.8% and solar PV 24.0% in 2025.

statement: Reactors connected to the grid in 2024 took a median 8.6 years to build.
detail: Seven units, from 61 months (Zhangzhou 1) to 204 (Flamanville 3); mean 114. In 2025, Zhangzhou 2 took 62 months.

statement: Uranium was discovered in 1789 and named after the newly found planet Uranus.
detail: Martin Klaproth found it in pitchblende eight years after Herschel spotted Uranus. Péligot first isolated the metal in 1841.

statement: Radioactivity was discovered in 1896 with a uranium salt and a photographic plate.
detail: Henri Becquerel's find. Hahn and Strassmann split the uranium atom in 1938; Meitner and Frisch explained fission in 1939.

statement: The first reactor, Chicago Pile-1, ran at half a watt on 2 December 1942.
detail: Fermi's team stacked 57 layers of graphite and natural uranium about 6 metres high. It later reached 200 watts.

statement: Nature built reactors first: 16 zones at Oklo, Gabon, about two billion years ago.
detail: Found in 1972. They pulsed for a few hundred thousand years at under 100 kW, burning about five tonnes of U-235.

statement: Uranium from about 20,000 Russian warheads became US reactor fuel between 1993 and 2013.
detail: 500 t of bomb-grade uranium was blended down into 14,446 t of fuel: about a third of US enrichment needs for 20 years.
calc: 14,446 t LEU / 500 t HEU = 28.9 t of fuel per tonne of HEU; ~150,000 t natural-uranium equivalent

statement: The glaze on vintage red Fiesta dinnerware was up to 14% uranium by weight.
detail: Made 1936-1943, then with depleted uranium 1959-1973; a plate holds about 4.5 g. Uranium glass, typically 2% uranium, glows green under UV.

statement: Switzerland's Beznau 1 has generated power since 1969: the longest-running reactor in service.
detail: Grid-connected 17 July 1969 and due to run until 2033. In the US, 25 reactors now hold licences to operate for 80 years.
calc: 2026 - 1969 = 57 years; 2033 - 1969 = 64 years at planned closure. India's Tarapur 1-2 also date from 1969 but sat idle 2020-2026.

statement: All US used fuel since the 1950s would cover one football field under 10 yards deep.
detail: About 90,000 tonnes (US DOE, 2022), growing by roughly 2,000 tonnes a year, stored at more than 70 sites in 35 states.
calc: Check: assemblies ~0.2 m x 0.2 m x 4.5 m = 0.18 m3 per ~0.5 t -> 90,000 t = 32,400 m3; / 4,459 m2 field = 7.3 m = 7.9 yards

statement: A 1 GWe reactor discharges about 27 tonnes of used fuel a year.
detail: About 26 t of it is still uranium, 1 t fission products and 0.3 t transuranics. As solid pellets, 2.5 cubic metres.
calc: 27.6 t UO2 / 10.97 t/m3 = 2.52 m3 (pellet volume only, not assemblies or casks)

statement: Nuclear's life-cycle emissions are about 6 grams of CO2 per kWh, the lowest UNECE found.
detail: UNECE range 5.1-6.4 g. Medians via Our World in Data: wind 11-17, solar PV 16-53, gas 439, coal 970. IPCC's 2014 nuclear median: 12.

statement: Nuclear causes about 0.03 deaths per TWh, roughly 800 times fewer than coal.
detail: Our World in Data, accidents plus air pollution, counting Chernobyl and Fukushima: coal 24.6, oil 18.4, gas 2.8, wind 0.04, solar 0.02.

statement: Per unit of electricity, nuclear needs about 50 times less land than coal.
detail: And 18 to 27 times less than ground-mounted solar, on UNECE life-cycle data. A 1,000 MW plant occupies about one square mile.
